new_statements.quote: The katu word has a main syllable which can be preceded by one, two, or three presyllables. The word can be symbolized as c3v/c2v/c1v/ MS. (Lower case is used for presyllable symbols, upper case for main syllable symbols.) The main syllable always receives the major stress. c3v and c2v are always affixes, and c1v sometimes is.
new_statements.citation: Wallace, Judith M. 1969. Katu phonemes. Mon-Khmer Studies 3: 64-73.
new_statements.locator: p. 69, section 3 'Word Structure and phoneme Distribution' (secondary remark p. 70)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. Opened (15-page image-only scan of MKS 3:61-75; Wallace's article is pp. 64-73 = file pages 4-13), rendered file page 9 (= MKS 3 p. 69) and read it as an image. Section 3 'Word Structure and phoneme Distribution' reads exactly: 'The katu word has a main syllable which can be precedeŋ by one, two, or three presyllables. The word can be symbolized as c3v/c2v/c1v/ MS. (Lower case is used for presyllable symbols, upper case for main syllable symbols.) The main syllable always receives the major stress. c3v and c2v are always affixes, and c1v sometimes is.2' Differences from the reported quote: the original prints 'precedeŋ' (a printer's error; the reader normalized it to 'preceded'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sesquisyllabic word: the main syllable, which is the last syllable of the word, always carries the major stress; the one to three preceding presyllables (mostly affixes, vowel /a/) are unstressed (p. 70: presyllable vowels 'usually actualize as an unstressed [ə]').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated; presyllables described as unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word = presyllable(s) + main syllable). IDENTITY: Wallace describes the Katu of Vietnam (Eastern Katu, east2332), not the Lao variety; the two Western-Katu descriptions opened (Costello & Sulavan 1996; Costello 1998) give the same presyllable + main-syllable structure (max two syllables in Lao) but contain no stress statement at all. Costello & Sulavan 1996 p. 233 treat the two as dialects with 'only a few predictable phonetic differences'.
new_statements.identity_note: The only explicit stress statement found (Wallace 1969, p. 69) describes the Katu of Quảng Nam/Thừa Thiên, Vietnam, which Glottolog files as Eastern Katu (east2332, ISO ktv), not Western Katu (west2398, kuf). The Western-Katu (Lao P.D.R.) descriptions by Costello (& Sulavan) 1996/1998 — 'Katu-L', Kalum district, Xe Kong province — are silent on stress, though they describe the same presyllable + main-syllable word (max two syllables in Laos) and say the two dialects differ by 'only a few predictable phonetic differences' (Costello & Sulavan 1996: 233); Choo 2012: 15-17 notes Costello never separates Eastern from Western Katu. A cataloguer may extend Wallace's rule to west2398 only as an inference; it is not a west2398 statement.
